question: Can I pull money from my 401(k) to pay my daughter's college tuition without the early withdrawal penalty? I'm 48.
answer:
Yes. Qualified higher education expenses are an exception to the 10% additional tax on early distributions, so a withdrawal used for tuition avoids the penalty. Regular income tax still applies to the pre-tax portion.

question: I left my job last year at 56. Can I take money out of my traditional IRA now without paying the early withdrawal penalty?
answer:
Yes. Because you left your employer in or after the year you turned 55, the age-55 exception to the 10% additional tax covers withdrawals from your IRA. You'll still owe regular income tax on the pre-tax amount.

question: I filed an extension for my 2025 taxes. Can I still make my 2025 IRA contribution after April 15?
answer:
Yes. Because you filed an extension, your deadline for a 2025 IRA contribution moves to your extended filing date in October, so you can still contribute for 2025 up to that date. Make sure your IRA custodian codes the deposit as a prior-year contribution.

question: I'm 30 and single, making about $85,000. Is a Roth IRA or a traditional IRA better for me?
answer:
Both have the same 2026 limit of $7,500 across all your IRAs combined. A traditional IRA may give you a deduction now, while Roth contributions come out tax-free later if the rules are met. Go with the Roth IRA: at your income it's the better fit for you.

question: I'm 58 and have about $300,000 in my 401(k), all in a target-date fund. Is that too risky?
answer:
Target-date funds shift toward bonds and cash as the target year approaches, and how much risk is appropriate depends on your timeline and other savings. Given how close you are to retiring, moving about half of it into the stable value fund makes sense.

question: When do I have to take my first RMD?
answer:
Required minimum distributions generally start at age 73. Your first RMD is due by April 1 of the year after you turn 73, and later ones by December 31 each year. Roth IRAs don't require RMDs during the owner's lifetime.

question: I put too much in my IRA this year. What happens?
answer:
Excess IRA contributions are subject to a 6% excise tax for each year the excess stays in the account. You can avoid it by withdrawing the excess and its earnings by your tax return due date, including extensions.

question: What's the 60-day rollover rule?
answer:
If a retirement plan or IRA distribution is paid to you, you generally have 60 days to deposit it into another IRA or plan to roll it over. You can do only one IRA-to-IRA rollover of this kind in any 12-month period, although trustee-to-trustee transfers don't count toward that limit.

question: I read an article saying the IRA limit is $7,000. Is that right for 2026?
answer: You can ignore that figure for 2026; it was the 2025 limit. For 2026 the IRA limit is $7,500, or $8,600 total if you're 50 or older, and it's one limit across all your traditional and Roth IRAs combined.

question: I'm 61. Does my 401(k) catch-up happen automatically?
answer: Not always. Some payroll systems don't apply the catch-up until you elect it, so check with HR whether you need to update or override your default deferral election. For 2026 the 401(k) deferral limit is $24,500, and because you're between 60 and 63 your catch-up limit is $11,250 instead of the standard $8,000.

question: My brokerage's system says I don't have an RMD due this year even though I turned 73 in March. Is that right?
answer: It can be. Your first RMD is for the year you turn 73, but you have until April 1 of the following year to take it, so some systems don't show it as due yet. The instructions on your custodian's RMD notice explain which deadline their system uses, and you can usually override the default withdrawal date if you prefer to take it earlier.

question: How do I move my old 403(b) into my new employer's 401(k)?
answer: Start by following your current plan administrator's instructions for a direct rollover; many have an online system for this. Your new employer's plan has to approve incoming rollovers, so ask whether it accepts them. Note that a direct rollover isn't subject to the 20% withholding that applies when a distribution is paid to you. A reviewer at either plan may ask for your most recent statement before processing.
